svg.aria-label: Network virtual appliance high availability: four designs, three deciding factors, and the health probe that drives failover
svg.title: Network virtual appliance high availability — four designs, three deciding factors, and the health probe behaviour behind them
svg.text: Network virtual appliances and high availability
Hub-and-spoke scope. Virtual WAN is excluded — it has more prescriptive NVA rules. Azure Firewall and
Application Gateway are Azure-native NVAs and use these same designs.
A single-instance SLA is not high availability
Instances “might shut down even if you configure them with Azure Premium SSDs, which provide a single-instance
service-level agreement.” Highly available applications require at least two NVAs — and in different availability
zones, with an Azure NAT gateway with availability zone support for egress.
Four designs against the three aspects Microsoft names: convergence time · topology · traffic symmetry
Design
Convergence
Topology
Traffic symmetry
Load Balancer
HA ports rule
10 to 15 seconds
Active/active, active/standby, scale-out
Not guaranteed — SNAT required
for stateful NVAs such as firewalls
Azure Route Server
requires BGP
BGP timers — 60s / 180s,
negotiable lower
Scale-out to 8 — max 8 BGP adjacencies
Not guaranteed — SNAT required
ECMP picks an instance per flow
Gateway Load Balancer
spans multiple VNets
10 to 15 seconds
Internet flows only — no East-West
no VNet peering, no workload UDRs
Guaranteed without SNAT
Dynamic public IP + UDRs
no NVA features needed
One to two minutes
8x the Load Balancer worst case
Active/passive only — scales up, not out
split brain possible
Guaranteed — one active instance
No design offers scale-out, symmetry and East-West together. A real hub often runs two of these, not one.
Symmetry is not a feature — it is how many load balancers a flow crosses
Single NIC, one internal load balancer
Both directions traverse the same load balancer,
so it “selects the same NVA instance for both
directions.”
Symmetry guaranteed, no SNAT, no extra work.
Dual NIC, internal LB in and public LB out
Each direction crosses a different load balancer.
Neither “can guarantee traffic symmetry,” so the
NVA must SNAT to attract return traffic.
Plus per-port rules: HA ports are inbound only.
The same SNAT #79 called damage — it hides the source address the perimeter was deployed to read — is here a
stated prerequisite. One mechanism, two names, depending on which requirement you arrived with.
The health probe is what actually decides failover
The default probe interval depends on how you deployed the load balancer
Azure portal default: every 5 seconds. ARM templates, REST API, Azure CLI, PowerShell: 15 seconds (minimum 5).
At a threshold of three failures that is 15 seconds of failure in the portal and 45 seconds by template — three
times the budget, with nothing in either resource looking misconfigured. The threshold is configurable too.
Probe source is always 168.63.129.16
Permitted by default via the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, so an NSG is rarely the cause. Do not use the
Microsoft-owned range containing it in a VNet, and do not block the probe with an NSG to test failover — that
is unsupported and can make NSG rules take delayed effect.
Because every probe comes from one address, a dual-NIC NVA “must send these health check responses back
through the same interface on which they're received” — typically multiple routing tables in the guest OS.
Never probe a port the appliance proxies
Probe a forwarded port and “any probe response from a single virtual machine marks down the appliance” — a
documented cascading failure where one unhealthy backend removes the perimeter. Probe the appliance itself,
and under an HA ports rule one probe response must reflect the status of the entire instance.
What the probe result does not tell you
“All instances down” does not mean traffic stopped
When every instance probes down, Standard Load Balancer sends no new flows to the pool but allows established
TCP flows to continue — given the pool has more than one instance. So an appliance the platform reports as dead
is still passing traffic, while all existing UDP flows terminate: DNS fails hard as TCP appears healthy.
A flapping probe earns a penalty of unstated length
“If the health probe fluctuates, the load balancer waits longer” — deliberate, and not quantified. The 10 to 15
second figure describes a clean failure, not a marginal appliance, so it is not a recovery-time objective.
And the article's own conclusion: “the most important aspect is whether the NVA vendor evaluates and validates
the design. The vendor must also provide the required NVA configuration.”
